newsitem.title: UK: UK's Labour drives home attack on Conservatives.
newsitem.headline: UK's Labour drives home attack on Conservatives.

text.p: Labour leader Tony Blair is due to keep up the pressure on the government on Tuesday, building on tough pledges to hold down tax and spending with the claim that Britain's new business generation is backing him.
With Britain due to hold a general election by May, opinion polls are tipping the Labour opposition to end the Conservatives' run of power that has lasted since 1979.

Labour's economics spokesman Gordon Brown wrong-footed the Conservatives on Monday by pledging that a Labour government would not raise basic or top tax rates for the five-year life of the next parliament or increase spending for at least two years.
With the critical question of tax -- which Labour believes lost it the last election -- wrapped up, Blair's speech is designed to flesh out the opposition party's business policies.

Using as a platform the launch of a report by business leaders on why Britain is not performing better, Blair will argue that Labour's efforts to improve links with the business community have moved beyond reassurance to partnership.

Citing a growing list of business backers and advisers, aides said he would say: "New Labour represents a new generation leading in British politics, allied to a new generation which is taking over the business establishment as well."
Aides said the growing support for Labour from the business community was worrying the Conservatives.
Ruling party aides quoted a report in the pro-Conservative Evening Standard on Monday saying Labour had failed to win over the hearts and minds of the old guard in the City of London.

But Brian Wilson, Labour's campaign spokesman, said the report -- based on a survey of business people who supported the Conservatives at the last election in 1992 -- included some who had since suffered business reversals or had retired.

Labour aides approvingly quoted the paper's Monday editorial that said Brown's cast-iron pledges on taxation and spending "could prove, with hindsight, to have provided the knockout blow to (British Prime Minister John) Major".

But Tuesday's British papers questioned whether Brown could stick to his promises. It could be too good to be true, the Times argued, "unless Mr Brown can changed entrenched Labour attitudes on public spending".

The Independent agreed. "Everyone suspects that the heart of old Labour still beats, and that the party's active instincts, when staff and servants are under strain, will be to cry out for more money as the obvious answer."
The Financial Times called Brown's promises "incredible" and noted he did not say he would keep the overall tax burden down.

The Times said real problems in limiting spending would come in 1998/1999. "Whether Labour's resolve would hold can only be tested in government. But success would be even less likely if Mr Brown had not said what he said yesterday," it said.
"With New Labour slaying the high-tax dragon (Major) needs a new monster to fight from his soapbox," the mass-circulation Sun said. It suggested a stronger anti-Europe stance would work.
Apart from the onslaught from Labour, Major's Conservatives face potential turmoil from their own ranks on Tuesday.

Conservative member of parliament Teresa Gorman, one of a band of rebels who want a harder line on Britain's role in the European Union, is introducing a bill demanding a referendum on whether to renegotiate British membership.
The bill has no chance of getting onto the statute books, but the test of Conservative party unity will be how many ruling party MPs efffectively defy Major and back the bill.
